tldr: The authors propose "SemPhys," a framework for humanoid motion generation from natural language that directly evaluates the robot's actual executed motion after controller tracking and optimizes the motion generator end-to-end through a differentiable local world model.
hero_caption: Overview of the SemPhys training framework. (a) A fixed controller executes the reference motion produced by the generator in simulation. (b) A differentiable world model reproduces a short segment from that recorded execution, which is re-inserted into the full sequence to backpropagate the overall semantic score. A paired anchoring loss to the initial model is also used to prevent the generator from collapsing.
overview:
When directing a humanoid to perform complex movements using natural language, a common approach is to first generate a geometric reference trajectory (kinematics) from text, and then pass it to a tracking controller trained via reinforcement learning for physical execution.

However, there is a major catch. To avoid falling, the controller prioritizes balance and contact constraints above all else, often cutting short or distorting the reference trajectory. For example, if you instruct it to "turn around and then walk," a controller on the verge of falling might cut the turn short and start walking early, sending the robot in a completely wrong direction. From a human perspective, this no longer counts as following the instructions.

To address this, the authors took an intuitive approach: semantic alignment must be evaluated directly on the motion the controller physically finishes executing. This is "SemPhys." The semantic evaluator scores the full trajectory executed in simulation, and its gradients are backpropagated to the motion generator through a differentiable world model (a lightweight model predicting local robot dynamics) and the tracking controller.

Evaluated on the BONES-SEED benchmark and a physical humanoid (Unitree G1), SemPhys achieved a text retrieval accuracy (R@1) of 79.62% on executed motions—outperforming prior state-of-the-art models by roughly 20 percentage points—while demonstrating remarkable stability with a fall rate of just 0.25‰.
contributions: Established a learning paradigm that evaluates semantic alignment between language instructions and the full trajectory physically executed by the robot, providing direct feedback to the motion generator.

Proposed the Contextual Execution Surrogate, a method that inserts a local differentiable prediction window into recorded simulator trajectories, allowing closed-loop control gradients to backpropagate while preserving full contextual history.

Introduced Paired Prior Anchoring to penalize divergence from the pre-trained generator's output under identical inputs, preserving motion diversity while drastically reducing training instability and fall risks.

Demonstrated on both simulation and a physical humanoid (Unitree G1) that semantic degradation caused by controller tracking is dramatically suppressed, enabling high-fidelity execution of complex composite instructions.

sections.heading: Why Doesn't the Robot Follow the Instruction Even When the Trajectory Does?
sections.summary: Generating motion trajectories from text often fails because tracking controllers alter movements to satisfy physical constraints and balance, destroying the original semantic intent. SemPhys evaluates semantics on the final executed outcome and refines the generator directly through a differentiable world model.
sections.details:
Imagine asking a humanoid to "turn around and walk forward." It is critical for the robot to perform both actions in order. If it begins walking before completing the turn, it will head in the wrong direction, even if the walking itself is stable.

Conventional text-to-motion models merely generate kinematic reference trajectories. On a physical robot, a whole-body controller drives the joints while maintaining balance, often truncating turns or aborting reaching motions to avoid falling. For instance, with the existing MotionGPT3 model, the generated reference trajectory achieves a semantic retrieval rate of $74.08\%$ against the instruction, but this plunges to $58.18\%$ once executed by the controller.

In other words, motion generation for robots is meaningless unless evaluated on the executed trajectory rather than the generated one. However, backpropagating through the entire physical execution pipeline inside a simulator is intractable due to computational cost and chaotic dynamics.

This is where SemPhys innovates. A differentiable world model predicts only a short window from the robot's recorded execution in simulation, which is then spliced back into the original trajectory before and after the window to evaluate the complete sequence. This preserves the surrounding context while successfully delivering gradients back to the generator through local dynamics. In experiments, SemPhys achieved an executed retrieval accuracy (R@1) of $79.62\%$, beating the strongest baseline MDM by about 20 percentage points, and confirmed successful execution of composite actions on a physical Unitree G1.

sections.heading: Physics-Aware Motion Generation and the Trend in Differentiable Dynamics
sections.summary: We review execution-aware approaches such as tracking-reward prediction, candidate reranking, and human preference learning. SemPhys sets itself apart by keeping the controller fixed and optimizing the generator directly for sequence-level semantic alignment via a differentiable world model.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into three lines of research.

### Execution-Aware Motion Generation
To make reference motions easier for controllers to track, prior methods have been proposed: RobotMDM predicts tracking rewards, TeXedo filters multiple candidates in simulation, and PhysMoDPO applies Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) based on execution outcomes. However, on composite instructions, cutting a turn short can ruin the heading for the entire subsequent walking phase, causing long-term semantic failure. SemPhys tackles this head-on by making local predictions of closed-loop control differentiable.

### Differentiable Dynamics and Generative Alignment
Simulating short horizons with learned dynamics models and using their gradients to update policies is common in reinforcement learning. Recent work like SuperMimic trains the controller using world models. SemPhys takes the inverse approach: it keeps the controller fixed and updates the text-to-motion generator. At deployment, the world model is discarded, and the robot simply tracks the high-quality generated reference using the existing controller.

### Kinematic Motion Generation and Whole-Body Control
Natural human motion generation has advanced rapidly with diffusion models (e.g., MDM) and discrete token models (e.g., MoMask, MotionGPT3). Robust whole-body tracking controllers trained via RL are also well-established. SemPhys bridges these cutting-edge generative models and control techniques using sequence-level text-motion matching.

sections.heading: Improving the Whole via Local Gradients: How SemPhys Works
sections.summary: SemPhys consists of three core components: semantic evaluation on executed trajectories, local surrogate gradients via a differentiable world model, and an anchoring constraint to the initial model. At deployment, it runs in real time without the world model.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Overview and Problem Formulation
The overall SemPhys architecture is shown in Figure F2. Given text instruction $c$ and noise $z$, a DiT-based (Diffusion Transformer) generator $G_\theta$ produces reference motion $X_\theta$. A fixed tracking controller $\pi_{\phi_0}$ executes this in simulation, yielding the actual executed trajectory $Y$. Our goal is to minimize the semantic discrepancy $d(c, Y)$ between the executed motion $Y$ and instruction $c$.

### 3.2 Semantic Alignment on Executed Motion
Alignment between language and motion is measured in a shared latent space using pre-trained text and motion encoders $E_t, E_m$. Feature vector $h_Y$ is extracted from the executed trajectory and $h_c$ from the instruction, minimizing their cosine distance $d^2 = 2 - 2\cos(h_Y, h_c)$. Because $Y$ is scored directly rather than reference $X_\theta$, the controller's balance-preserving adjustments are naturally accounted for.

### 3.3 Contextual Execution Surrogate
Backpropagating through an entire long trajectory inside a physics simulator is intractable. SemPhys instead uses a learned differentiable world model $f_\psi$ and the fixed controller in a closed loop to reproduce only a short window of length $H$ (32 steps = 0.64 seconds) from the simulation log.

The crucial design choice is that this predicted window is not evaluated in isolation. It is inserted back between the recorded "prefix" and "suffix" to reconstruct the full 6-second sequence before computing the overall semantic score. This preserves temporal context (such as whether the robot turned before walking) while cleanly passing gradients through the predicted window back to the generator's parameters.

### 3.4 Paired Prior Anchoring
Unconstrained optimization can lead the generator to output erratic motions that induce falls. To prevent this, SemPhys adds an anchoring penalty $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}}$ against the initial generator $G_{\theta_0}$ using the exact same text prompt $c$ and noise $z$. Pairing identical noise inputs strongly restrains optimization drift without collapsing generative diversity.

During inference and hardware deployment, neither the world model nor the semantic evaluator is needed. The controller simply tracks trajectories from the updated generator, executing high-fidelity motions with zero added compute overhead.

captions.F2: Detailed architecture of SemPhys. (a) The controller tracks the generator's reference motion in simulation. (b) A differentiable world model unrolls a 32-step window from that log, spliced with fixed surrounding trajectory context to compute full-action semantic alignment and anchoring loss, updating only the generator's projection heads.

sections.heading: Verified on Benchmark and Hardware: Eliminating Semantic Drift and Slashing Falls
sections.summary: Evaluations on the BONES-SEED dataset and a physical Unitree G1 show that SemPhys achieves an executed R@1 of 79.62%, outperforming existing methods by a wide margin while demonstrating strong robustness against physical parameter variations.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on the test split of the humanoid benchmark BONES-SEED (13,302 clips, including 13,082 upright tasks). Baselines evaluated with the same Unitree G1 controller include MDM, MoMask, MotionGPT3, TeXedo, and OMG. Metrics include instruction retrieval accuracy (R@1 to R@3), text-motion embedding distance (MM), feature distribution distance for motion realism (FID), and persistent fall rate per thousand upright tasks (Fail).

### 4.2 Main Comparison Results
SemPhys achieved an executed R@1 of $79.62\%$, surpassing the strongest baseline MDM ($60.10\%$) by 19.52 points. It also showed remarkable stability with a fall rate of only $0.25$ ‰ (roughly 2.5 falls per 10,000 runs). In a blind study with 10 human evaluators, SemPhys ranked highest in both naturalness (2.44/3) and semantic alignment (2.68/3).

Particularly notable is the preservation of semantic fidelity under tracking. While MotionGPT3's R@1 dropped from $74.08\%$ on reference motions to $58.18\%$ on executed motions (a nearly 16-point drop), SemPhys experienced a mere 1.04-point decrease, from $80.63\%$ to $79.59\%$.

### Robustness and Qualitative Results
Across 16 perturbation conditions varying robot mass, actuator strength, and ground friction, SemPhys maintained an average R@1 of $78.89\%$ and Fail of $0.70$ ‰. As illustrated in Figure F6, for a "pick up an object from low ground" prompt, other methods either fell over or skipped bending down; SemPhys maintained balance while bending deeply to complete the motion. On the physical Unitree G1, the policy trained purely in simulation executed turns and forward walking smoothly without extra tuning.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies
Testing the importance of supervision in execution space revealed that computing the same loss on reference trajectories yielded an R@1 of only $74.21\%$, highlighting the roughly 5-point advantage of SemPhys's execution-space evaluation ($79.30\%$). Removing Paired Prior Anchoring caused the fall rate to spike over 20-fold, from $0.25$ ‰ to $6.09$ ‰, with high variance across seeds.

Furthermore, as shown in Figure F8, evaluating the 32-step window alone gave an R@1 of $64.88\%$, and padding boundaries gave $68.07\%$. Inserting the window into the recorded prefix and suffix (SemPhys's ordered context) boosted accuracy to $79.31\%$. Maintaining global context while calculating local gradients proved to be a critical architectural choice.

captions.F6: Qualitative comparison of motion execution. (a) For "pick up from low ground," MotionGPT3 falls forward and TeXedo skips bending, whereas SemPhys bends deeply while maintaining posture. (b) For "turn around and carry," only SemPhys completes both turning and walking while sustaining the carrying posture.
captions.F8: Comparison of context formats fed to the semantic evaluator during training. Evaluating only the 32-step window (top) or padding endpoints (middle) underperforms, whereas SemPhys's Ordered context (bottom), which splices the prediction into recorded trajectories, achieves the highest executed R@1 (79.31%).

sections.heading: Conclusion: A New Standard for Making Humanoids Follow Instructions to the Letter
sections.summary: SemPhys is a pioneering framework that aligns physically executed humanoid motions with language instructions. Combining a local differentiable world model, context preservation, and paired anchoring achieves both expressive motion generation and physical stability.
sections.details:
In humanoid control, physical constraints have long created a wide gap between intended ideal trajectories and executed physical outcomes. SemPhys bridges this divide by cleverly using a differentiable world model to train the motion generator directly on executed semantics.

Computing closed-loop control gradients over a short temporal window and embedding it into the full episode context elegantly balances computational tractability with semantic accuracy. Additionally, the paired prior anchoring loss prevents optimization drift and physical instability.

Deploying on the physical Unitree G1 without additional fine-tuning demonstrates the high practical utility of this framework. Future work points naturally toward richer interactions with the environment and tasks involving dynamic obstacle avoidance.

takeaways: Evaluating motion generation on kinematic references leads to semantic failure due to controller corrections; evaluations must be performed on physically tracked, executed trajectories.

Instead of differentiating through an entire episode, inserting a short differentiable prediction window between recorded context trajectories enables stable gradient backpropagation while preserving long-term temporal semantics.
Paired Prior Anchoring, which penalizes divergence from the initial generator given identical prompts and random noise, serves as a powerful regularizer to prevent falls and stabilize training.
Using the world model only during training and reverting to standard tracking with a fixed controller during inference yields significant performance gains without any runtime compute overhead.
limitations: Gradients rely on the world model's predictive fidelity; under extreme contact conditions where simulator physics and world model predictions diverge, gradient reliability may degrade.
Optimization was restricted to updating projection heads; scalability and stability when fine-tuning the entire generator backbone remain unverified.

Evaluations focused primarily on flat-ground walking, turning, and upper-body gestures; extending to complex environmental interactions such as stairs, rough terrain, or external object contacts remains future work.
